items.title: Human and Organizational Factors
items.abstract: This chapter examines the evidence base for human and organizational factors (HOF) as an approach to managing OSH, critically evaluating its theoretical coherence, its practical distinctiveness, and its field-validated impact on injury reduction. It describes HOF as an eclectic, sociotechnical integrative domain drawing from industrial, occupational, organizational psychology, ergonomics, and sociology, while noting that it lacks unique practical interventions and operates primarily as a knowledge broker rather than a distinct scientific discipline. The chapter highlights HOF&s;s reliance on non-falsifiable, post-hoc interpretive frameworks, and its problematic dismissal of human error as a valid root cause in incident investigations. Drawing on the available field studies across human factors engineering, ergonomics, human performance improvement, and sociological approaches to safety, it provides practitioners with a critical evidence-based appraisal of HOF, concluding that its claimed contributions to OSH exceed what the field-validated evidence currently supports.

items.title: Human in Control: A Practical Framework for Evaluating Human Control of Advanced AI Agents
items.abstract: This working paper proposes the Human Control Model, a six-dimension framework for evaluating measurable human control of advanced AI agents: Intervention Durability, Technical Containment, Informed Delegation, Oversight Integrity, Control Contagion, and Situational Grounding. It separates behavioral severity from environment reality so that simulations and controlled evaluations are not presented as real-world incidents. Five pilot reviews, HIC-001 through HIC-005, illustrate control-specific measures including detection-to-containment time, permission comprehension gap, monitor independence, and instruction provenance integrity. An additional qualitative stress test informed framework refinement; it is not independent validation. The Meta case is based on a reported user account, with permission history, causal interpretation, and severity remaining provisional. The framework is conceptual and case-based, without inter-rater reliability testing or validated quantitative thresholds. Version 1.0.1 corrects source wording, incorporates the recovered HIC-0 through HIC-5 definitions, and clarifies evidence limitations. Creator: Human in Control Project. License: CC BY 4.0. items.title: Human Libraries in Teacher Education: Exploring Pre-Service Teachers’ Narratives of Perceived Change Through Thinking Routines
items.abstract: The main objective of this study is to explore how pre-service teachers retrospectively describe differences between their prior and current perspectives following participation in a Human Library. This research begins with a review of the literature on the definition and characteristics of Human Libraries and proceeds with the creation of one in a university setting. To this end, the study benefited from the collaboration of the Baketik Foundation, which facilitated contact with five individuals willing to share their testimonies on topics related to human rights. The initial sample consisted of 53 pre-service teachers in the Early Childhood Education Bachelor’s programme at the University of the Basque Country (EHU), although ultimately, following a screening process, the sample was reduced to 51. Data were collected using the “I used to think…/Now I think…” reflection exercise, which the pre-service teachers were asked to complete after listening to the testimonies. The narratives were first examined manually by the researchers to identify recurring ideas and potential thematic categories. Microsoft Copilot and ChatGPT were subsequently used to support the identification and consistency checking of the initial category structure, while the final coding was conducted manually by the researchers. Six thematic categories were identified in both sections of the reflection exercise. The descriptive comparison revealed differences in the frequency and elaboration of participants’ narratives, particularly regarding empathy and changes in perspective, peace and social justice, women’s rights and gender-based violence, and silence, social taboos and lack of awareness. Because both sections were produced retrospectively after the Human Library experience, these differences are interpreted as features of participants’ accounts rather than as direct evidence of objectively measured changes in their perspectives.

items.title: Human-centered industry 5.0 technologies for occupational risk reduction: a systematic review
items.abstract: Introduction The transition to Industry 5.0 is transforming manufacturing through the integration of smart technologies, while simultaneously increasing the need to protect workers’ health and reduce occupational risks. This systematic review synthesized cross-sectoral evidence on human-centered Industry 5.0 technologies for assessing and reducing occupational risks, with a focus on ergonomic outcomes, worker-related factors, and the conditions influencing their implementation and transferability. Methods A systematic literature search was conducted in Scopus and Web of Science following the PRISMA 2020 framework and predefined eligibility criteria based on PECO. Included studies were analyzed according to technology type, occupational risk addressed, ergonomic dimension, assessment method, reported outcomes, implementation conditions, and implications for occupational health and safety, yielding a total of 78 studies that met the inclusion criteria. Results The reported results from individual studies included ergonomic assessment accuracies exceeding 95%, fatigue reductions of more than 50% in selected applications, and cycle-time reductions of up to 28.4%, along with improvements in task allocation, workload monitoring, and production efficiency. These values should not be interpreted as overall effects of Industry 5.0 technologies, given the heterogeneity of technologies, experimental designs, and assessment methods. Discussion The evidence was limited by laboratory validation, a lack of longitudinal research, heterogeneous assessment methods, and insufficient real-world implementation in specific industrial sectors.

items.title: Human-centric digital twins in industry 5.0: technologies, applications, and future directions
items.abstract: Industry 5.0 (I5.0) emphasizes industrial technologies that are human-centric, sustainable, and resilient. Human-Centric Digital Twins (HCDTs) support this transition by integrating worker data with robots, machines, tasks, and industrial environments. However, the relevant research remains fragmented across human modelling, Human–Robot Collaboration, Artificial Intelligence (AI), simulation, and Digital Twin (DT) research. Moreover, systems that use human data or adaptive automation are often described as human-centric without demonstrating measurable benefits to workers. This review addresses these limitations by distinguishing HCDTs from conventional human models, Human DTs, and collaborative robotic systems. It critically examines human-focused sensing, multi-modal data integration, biomechanical modelling, intention and motion prediction, robotic simulation, optimization, reinforcement learning, immersive interfaces, industrial connectivity, and data governance. Based on this analysis, a literature-derived conceptual framework is proposed that connects sensing, integration, human modelling, analytics, simulation, decision-making, adaptation, human interaction, and governance. The framework organizes the functional requirements of HCDTs and is intended to inform future system design and comparison; its practical applicability and effectiveness require further validation. The review argues that HCDTs must extend beyond worker monitoring and productivity maximization: human data should inform industrial decisions that produce measurable improvements in safety, ergonomics, wellbeing, autonomy, accessibility, or skill development. Such systems should also uphold privacy, transparency, uncertainty awareness, explainability, and appropriate human authority. By linking technological capabilities to explicit worker outcomes, this synthesis enables researchers and engineers to assess the human-centeredness of HCDT implementations and supports the development of trustworthy systems for I5.0.

items.title: Human–AI Collaboration as a New Governance Paradigm? Unpacking China’s Land Policy Responses to Environmental Pressures and Digital Transformation
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly embedded in land governance, reshaping how environmental pressures and sustainability goals are addressed. Yet the institutional processes through which human–AI collaboration takes shape remain largely unexplored. This study examines whether human–AI collaboration is emerging as a new governance paradigm in China’s land sector, and if so, through what institutional pathways and practical forms it is being articulated and implemented. Drawing on a systematic analysis of 352 policy documents and case studies from coastal regions, the study develops and applies the CTI framework—an analytical lens that integrates Contextual conditions, Technological capabilities, and Institutional arrangements. The findings reveal three interrelated developments: (1) policy discourse constructs a coherent narrative in which environmental pressures and digital transformation jointly create an imperative for change; (2) a systematic division of labor between AI and human officials emerges in policy and is reflected in practice, with AI handling data processing and preliminary screening while humans retain final decision-making, value judgment, and accountability; and (3) this division is being institutionalized through a staged process of policy guidance, pilot mechanisms, and institutional adaptation. These developments suggest that human–AI collaboration may be taking shape as an emerging governance paradigm in land governance, one that is beginning to be codified and tested in policy and practice. The study contributes an integrative analytical framework, specifies the logic of human–machine division of labor, and extends collaborative governance theory beyond its traditional human-centric assumptions. The findings also carry implications for governance contexts where human–AI collaboration is reshaping land governance and other policy domains.

items.title: Humanoid-human Collaboration in Understanding Implications of Driving Under Influence of Drugs: Systematic Review Versus Artificial Intelligence
items.abstract: Abstract This research involved co-creating a systematic review analysis alongside the world’s smartest humanoid robot, Ami. The work involved a human-humanoid collaboration in understanding driving under the influence of drugs’ (DUIDs’) prevalence, implications and chemical analysis. The systematic review was conducted according to the preferred reporting items for systematic reviews and meta-analysis guidelines. Quantitative studies reporting drugs encountered in DUID published between 2007 – 2025 were included. Studies that had no confirmatory chemical analysis were excluded. Included studies ( n = 25) were analysed independently by researchers and integrated into Ami’s knowledge-based system. Ami deployed large language models for analysis but often needed prompt to extract information. The results showed similarity in extraction between the systematic review and the humanoid analysis. Both approaches confirmed key drugs reported in DUID were alcohol, cannabinoids, cocaine, amphetamine, benzodiazepines, and opiates. Such drugs were often detected in blood and urine and less occasionally in oral fluid. Key techniques employed for their analysis were immunoassay, gas chromatography-mass spectrometry, and liquid chromatography-mass spectrometry, where the latter was the most sensitive technique. Implications of these drugs on driving included impairment, increased risk of accidents, with fatal accidents less frequent but more severe. No AI hallucinations were encountered in Ami’s answers; yet, examples were used from outside the studies integrated into the knowledge-based system. This showed that the humanoid is integrating experience and knowledge from other sourcing and adapting them in the present study. In summary, the humanoid offered a valuable and quick tool in analysis and can support healthcare research.

items.title: HYBRID QUANTUM-CLASSICAL LEARNING FRAMEWORK FOR INTELLIGENT FEATURE OPTIMIZATION AND PREDICTIVE ANALYTICS IN ENGINEERING APPLICATIONS
items.abstract: As the dimensionality and complexity of engineering data grows, traditional machine learning systems become increasinglydifficult to apply, especially when detecting informative features without sacrificing predictive accuracy and computationalefficiency. In this paper we proposed a Hybrid Quantum-Classical Learning Framework for Intelligent Feature Optimization andPredictive Analytics in Engineering Applications. The framework is a combination of classical data preprocessing, intelligentfeature selection, quantum-enhanced feature representation, parameterized quantum circuits and predictive learning in a unifiedoptimization pipeline. Engineering features are first normalized and evaluated to find informative subsets and minimizeredundancy. These selected features are then mapped onto the quantum feature space and parameterized quantum circuits tocreate improved representations for predictive modeling. The optimization objective takes into account predictive loss, size ofthe feature subset and regularization to achieve an efficient feature configuration. This quantum-classical representation is fed to the classical predictive models for classification and evaluation of the models. The framework is assessed based on predictiveaccuracy, ROC properties, feature reduction, convergence behavior, computational time, scalability and prediction error. Thepotential of using intelligent feature optimization combined with quantum enhanced representation for engineering analytics isillustrated by comparing it to conventional machine learning and hybrid learning models. This study provides a flexibleframework that enables the merging of quantum and classic machine learning, and shows how hybrid architectures can be usedin high-dimensional engineering prediction.

items.title: Hybridity for organizational learning
items.abstract: Abstract Hybrid approaches can help organizational actors learn and adjust to feedback. This chapter explores the knowledge-based view of organizations, which describes how organizations integrate knowledge from internal and external actors and rely on both explicit and tacit knowledge. Hybrid organizing enables organizational learning and innovation by integrating diverse logics and perspectives. Social impact organizers can cultivate hybrid synergy and productive tension by adopting mindset-shaping strategies that recognize both contradiction and complementarity. Examples from research and real life show how social impact organizers use hybridity to adapt and survive in turbulent environments and suggest an emerging area of research in human–artificial intelligence partnerships for social impact organizing.

items.title: Hyperlet Transform-Based Cognitive Load Assessment Using Single-Channel fNIRS Signals
items.abstract: Abstract Cognitive load assessment using functional nearinfrared spectroscopy (fNIRS) has gained increasing attention due to its non-invasive and high spatial resolution nature. However, reliable classification remains challenging due to non-stationary and nonlinear nature of haemodynamic signals. Conventional time-frequency representation methods often fails to capture subtle amplitude variations from haemodynamic responses due to limited joint time-frequency resolutions. In this study, an attempt has been made to characterize and estimate cognitive load using single-channel fNIRS and Hyperlet Transform (HLT). The framework integrates preprocessing, HLT based time-frequency decomposition, multidomain feature extraction, and optimal feature selection within a Leave-One-Subject-Out (LOSO) folds to identify robust biomarkers. The extracted features are applied to five ML classifiers namely SVM-RBF, KNN, Naive Bayes, AdaBoost, and Random Forest. Among the evaluated classifiers, Support Vector Machine with a Radial Basis Function kernel achieved highest performance with an accuracy of 73.33% for 3-class tasks, followed by 86.67% and 90.00% for Baseline vs Low and Baseline vs High Cognitive Load tasks. Further, HLT outperformed conventional time-frequency methods, which emphasizes that HLT derived features effectively capture cognitive workload related hemodynamic changes and provides strong potential for development of real-time deployable solutions for next-generation affective computing systems.

items.title: Hyperspectral imaging and machine learning in brain tumor surgery: Current evidence, clinical applications, and future directions
items.abstract: Background: Brain tumor surgery aims to achieve maximal safe resection while preserving neurological function; however, accurate intraoperative discrimination between tumor tissue and normal brain remains a major challenge. Hyperspectral imaging (HSI) has emerged as a promising label-free optical imaging modality that provides quantitative information on tissue biochemical and physiological characteristics. The integration of machine learning (ML) has further enhanced its potential for automated tissue classification and real-time intraoperative decision support. This narrative review summarizes the current evidence regarding HSI and ML in brain tumor surgery, highlighting technological principles, clinical applications, current limitations, and future directions. Methods: This narrative review was based on a comprehensive literature search of PubMed, Scopus, and Google Scholar to identify studies evaluating the application of HSI and artificial intelligence (AI) in brain tumor surgery. The search strategy included combinations of the keywords “ hyperspectral imaging ,” “ brain tumor ,” “ glioma ,” “ machine learning ,” “ deep learning ,” “ artificial intelligence ,” and “ neurosurgery .” Priority was given to peer-reviewed original research articles, narrative and systematic reviews, and clinically relevant investigations describing the technical development, intraoperative application, and translational potential of HSI in neurooncology. Landmark studies that established the foundations of HSI, together with recent publications reflecting advances in ML and clinical implementation, were preferentially included to provide both historical context and contemporary perspectives. Manual screening of the reference lists of key publications was performed to identify additional relevant studies. As a narrative review, this manuscript was intended to provide a critical overview of current evidence rather than a systematic assessment of the literature. Consequently, no formal study selection algorithm, quality assessment tool, or quantitative meta-analysis was performed. Results: Current evidence indicates that HSI combined with ML enables accurate intraoperative tissue classification, improved tumor margin delineation, and emerging molecular characterization, including prediction of isocitrate dehydrogenase mutation status. Deep learning approaches generally outperform conventional ML techniques by integrating spectral and spatial information. Although early clinical studies have demonstrated encouraging diagnostic performance, widespread implementation remains limited by heterogeneous imaging protocols, relatively small patient cohorts, limited multicenter validation, and computational challenges. Conclusion: HSI represents a promising adjunct for precision-guided brain tumor surgery by providing real-time biochemical tissue characterization without the need for exogenous contrast agents. Continued advances in AI, standardized imaging protocols, multicenter clinical validation, and multimodal intraoperative integration will be essential to facilitate routine clinical adoption and establish its impact on surgical and patient outcomes.

The v4.1 safeguards strengthen: evidence provenance and claim-status separation; distinction between observation, event, class, membership and mechanism; separation of hypothesized mechanisms from established structural conditions; treatment of UNRESOLVED versus supported negative claims; evidential dependency and uncertainty propagation; causal-status calibration; requirements for assigning Situated Selectivity (I); synthesis and intervention constraints. The release candidate underlying v4.1 was frozen and tested in a controlled cross-model Hessdalen regression using Claude, ChatGPT and Gemini. items.title: IAUC Systematic Literature Review: Extraction Protocol, Metadata, and Validation Data
items.abstract: Data and code for a systematic review of the urban climate literature. A large language model extracted structured information from the full text of every paper, and domain experts checked a sample of that extraction. This package lets you check the data and rebuild the paper's statistics, tables and figures. Start here Read README.md first. make check checks your setup. uv sync --extra dev installs the pinned environment, make paper-all rebuilds the statistics and tables, make figures draws the figures, and make ci-test runs the tests. No API keys are needed. data/README.md explains which values came from the model, which from fixed code, and which from the experts. Contents data/extracted_metadata/: 9,284 records, one per paper, as the model extracted them data/enrichments/ and data/contribution_rationales/: 9,284 records each of values computed from the extraction, and the reasoning behind each contribution label data/volunteer_review/: the anonymized expert review responses from both validation rounds, and the record of how a third reviewer settled the disagreements in the blind second round data/cross_model_validation/: comparisons with other models that support the choice of extraction model data/experiments/recall_audit_2025/: the search-recall audit, with its query strings, per-journal counts and the screening decision for each extra paper, and the check of how papers were assigned to publication years, with the corrected annual series data/contribution_reproducibility/: the earlier contribution labels the revision table is checked against, and the contribution classifier's attestation and the production promotion manifest that binds it src/, tests/, Makefile and uv.lock: the analysis code and its tests License Everything in this deposit, data and code alike, is released under CC-BY-4.0. This version Final archive for the accepted manuscript. Compared with version 4.0 (23 September 2026), the extracted records and the set of papers are unchanged. Each paper's world region and income group are now joined on ISO 3166 country codes rather than on country names, which fills them in for 236 records whose country names had not matched (mostly studies in Turkey, Taiwan and the Netherlands); country names in the enrichment records follow ISO 3166, and figures and tables use short names such as Iran, South Korea and Vietnam. The inclusion validation now covers all 999 reviewed papers (one had been dropped by a file-name encoding mismatch), so agreement is 867 of 999 (86.8%), and the method-flag concordance figures are updated to match. The method-combination figure now counts every combination, including machine-learning models used alone.

items.title: Immuno-metabolic crosstalk in osteoarthritis: from mechanisms to therapies
items.abstract: Background Osteoarthritis (OA) is a heterogeneous whole-joint disorder influenced by mechanical stress, aging, previous trauma, genetic susceptibility, subchonrral bone alterations, and localized inflamation.Emerging evidence suggests that immune and metabolic processes alterations may be involved in OA pathogenesis particularly in inflammatory and metabolically dysregulated subtypes. Content This narrative review summarizes the bidirectional crosstalk between immune and metabolic processes during OA progression. Human observational studies and experimental models suggest that immune-cell activation and metabolic dysfunction may interact to influence synovial inflammation and cartilage homeostasis although their causal relevance and relative contributions vary across OA phenotypes. We further discuss emerging immunometabolic strategies targeting glycolytic and lipid-metabolic pathways as well as predominantly experimental approaches involving gene editing synthetic biology and stem cell-based therapies. Conclusion Integrating multi-omics technologies with personalized medicine may improve patient stratification and dynamic monitoring and could facilitate the future development of more personalized and potentially disease-modifying strategies for OA.Future research should focus on clarifying the dynamic immunometabolic network underlying OA and promoting the clinical translation of innovative strategies through artificial intelligence and interdisciplinary collaboration.

items.title: Impact of AI Exposure on the Development of English Language Skills: A Single-Participant Case Study-Based Investigation
items.abstract: Developing English language skills in ESL learners is a long-experienced challenge for teachers and the learners. In this scenario, consistent interaction with artificial intelligence (AI) tools capable of orchestrating authentic interactions with the language is found to be useful in facilitating learners to acquire and master of English language skills. Such tools have the potential to create opportunities for learners to achieve personalised and interactive learning experiences, enable teachers to provide individualised feedback, and open avant-garde adaptive pathways for learning. Additionally, they may promote learners’ motivation, encourage their active participation, and engage them in self-directed learning procedures. Therefore, this exploratory single-participant case study aims to investigate whether exposure to AI has a positive impact on developing English language skills. The data were collected using a qualitative case study focused on an academic in a public university in Sri Lanka. The data collection methods included semi-structured interviews, document analysis, and observations. The results obtained during the action research and empirical study indicated that consistent interaction with AI tools facilitates the acquisition of English language skills and enables individuals to use them confidently in authentic situations.

items.title: IMPACT OF AI-ENABLED HR PRACTICES ON ORGANIZATIONAL BEHAVIOUR AND EMPLOYEE PERFORMANCE
items.abstract: Human resource management (HRM) is being transformed by artificial intelligence (AI). Organisations increasingly use AI to screen applicants, schedule interviews, personalise learning, provide continuous performance feedback, predict attrition, answer employee queries and allocate work. These AI-enabled HR practices promise efficiency, consistency and personalisation, but they also alter the relationship between employees and the organisation in ways that shape attitudes, behaviours and performance. This chapter examines the impact of AI-enabled HR practices on organisational behaviour and employee performance. It first clarifies the concepts of electronic HRM, HR analytics, algorithmic HRM and AI-enabled HRM and traces their evolution. It then reviews AI applications across the HR value chain, from workforce planning and recruitment to learning, performance management, compensation, engagement, retention and HR service delivery. Drawing on the ability–motivation–opportunity framework, social exchange theory, organisational justice theory, the job demands–resources model, psychological contract theory and technology acceptance theories, the chapter explains the mechanisms through which AI-enabled HR practices influence trust, perceived fairness, engagement, job satisfaction, autonomy, technostress, job insecurity and, ultimately, task, contextual and innovative performance. A synthesis of empirical evidence shows that effects are contingent: AI-enabled HR practices tend to improve outcomes when they are transparent, fair, augmentative and supported by leadership, and to undermine them when they are opaque, controlling or perceived as reductive. The chapter proposes an integrative conceptual framework with research propositions, discusses ethical and legal considerations, including India’s Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023, and offers practical guidance for managers.

items.title: Impact of Different Technologies Used in Enhancing Astro Tourism
items.abstract: Astronomy and space are undergoing a transformation in how they are explored and understood by human visitors, thanks to technologies such as artificial intelligence (AI), augmented reality (AR), virtual reality (VR), satellite imaging, mobile applications, smart telescopes, and astrophotography devices. Mobile Sky Mapping Applications allow visitors to find planets, stars, and constellations in real time. Weather predictions, visibility updates, and customized tips for optimal viewing conditions are all possible with AI systems. Similarly, AR and VR technologies can offer a virtual experience by generating simulated space and astronomical phenomena, enabling tourists to virtually travel through space to explore galaxies and planets that would be impossible to reach in the real world. Telescopes have become more accessible to amateur astronomers and tourists, thanks to new telescope technology and automated observatories. Satellite technology is utilized to help determine areas with dark skies and reduced light pollution. These technologies enhance tourists’ engagement and learning, raise scientific awareness, help protect the environment, and boost economic opportunities for tourism areas in remote regions. The results of this study point to the potential of different technologies to transform astro tourism and offer new, educational, and immersive experiences worldwide.

items.title: Implementing a Course-Specific Chatbot in Undergraduate Biochemistry
items.abstract: Abstract Generative artificial intelligence (AI) tools are increasingly available to students, but their educational value depends on how they are configured, constrained, and integrated into course practices. This technology report describes a no-code workflow for implementing a course-specific chatbot in upper-division undergraduate biochemistry using a custom GPT configured with instructor-generated lecture slides, class transcripts, handouts, syllabus information, and custom instructions. The workflow emphasized course alignment, frequent updating, instructor validation, assessment scoping, and student prompt guidance. The chatbot was used in biochemistry I lecture across two consecutive fall offerings and extended to biochemistry II lecture for follow-up use. Student survey responses indicated substantial adoption and generally positive perceptions; peer-led supplemental instruction attendance and course-grade data are presented only as contextual information. The report highlights a practical, transferable approach for using no-code custom GPT tools to extend course-aligned study support while preserving instructor oversight and existing academic support structures.

items.title: Improving market infrastructure for small entrepreneurship in Uzbekistan: a sociological opinion on export potential, employment, and social inclusion
items.abstract: Uzbekistan has moved further and faster on small-business reform than most countries in the post-Soviet region. Between 2017 and 2025 the share of small business in GDP rose from roughly one third to over half, and the number of registered small entities reached 1.21 million by October 2025 (State Statistics Agency, 2025). The country was recognised as one of the five largest global improvers in the 2024 Women, Business and the Law index, with an 11.9-point gain taking its score to 82.5 (World Bank, 2024). The Uzbekistan-2030 strategy targets a doubling of exports and an increase in the number of exporting enterprises from roughly 5,700 to 15,000 (Ministry of Investment and Foreign Trade, 2024).These figures have been read almost exclusively through an economic and engineering lens. The dominant policy frame treats market infrastructure as a matter of roads, customs procedures, payment systems, credit lines and digital platforms. That frame is not wrong. It is incomplete in a specific and consequential way, and the way it is incomplete is sociological. This article makes a conceptual argument rather than reporting new data. Our contribution is not the observation that markets are socially embedded, which has been established since Polanyi (1944) and Granovetter (1985). It is threefold and more specific.First, we argue that the social layer of market infrastructure should be treated as infrastructure in its own right, not as context surrounding the "real" infrastructure. This extends to a post-Soviet setting the argument developed by Elyachar (2010) for Cairo, where the communicative channels produced by women's everyday sociality function as economic infrastructure in the same register as roads and telephone lines, and it connects that argument to Star's (1999) and Larkin's (2013) insistence that infrastructure is relational and becomes visible only through the practices that sustain or fail to sustain it.Second, we specify the mechanism by which social structure acts on formally universal infrastructure. We call it differential access filtering, and we decompose it using the four sources of social capital distinguished by Portes and Sensenbrenner (1993), namely value introjection, bounded solidarity, reciprocity exchanges and enforceable trust. Two of these enable market participation and two constrain it, which gives the framework an internal reason to expect both positive and negative effects rather than asserting one or the other.Third, we propose Uzbekistan as a scope condition for embeddedness theory. Most of the informality and embeddedness literature has examined settings where formal institutions were weak, absent or decaying (Mair and Martí, 2009;Williams and Shahid, 2016). Uzbekistan presents the inverse configuration, in which formal market infrastructure is being built rapidly and from above onto a dense, legally codified communal institution. The theoretical question this raises is whether embeddedness under rapid state-led formalisation produces bridging or closure, and our answer is that it systematically produces both, with the balance determined by which of the four mechanisms a given reform activates.The article proceeds as follows. Section 2 develops the theoretical framing. Section 3 sets out the fivelayer framework and its social mediators. Section 4 reads the mahalla symmetrically. Section 5 applies the framework differentially to five entrepreneurial positions. Section 6 states explicitly what the available evidence does and does not support. Section 7 discusses feasibility of the policy implications. Section 8 sets out the theoretical contribution, limitations, testable propositions and research agenda.Infrastructure studies in sociology and anthropology have moved decisively away from treating infrastructure as a stock of physical assets. Star (1999) argued that infrastructure is relational rather than substantive, that it is embedded in other structures and practices, and that its distributional properties become visible mainly at the point of breakdown. Larkin (2013) extended this by treating infrastructures as objects that carry political and aesthetic meaning as well as goods, and by showing that the promise attached to an infrastructure is part of what it does. Graham and Marvin (2001) documented the process by which networked infrastructure, far from producing uniform access, splinters into premium and residual circuits. Elyachar (2010) took the argument one step further in a way that is directly relevant here. Studying microfinance and empowerment projects in Cairo, she showed that the communicative channels generated by women's routine sociality constitute a social infrastructure that carries economic traffic as surely as a road does, and that development interventions make this infrastructure visible precisely by attempting to capture or format it. We take this as our starting point. If social ties are infrastructure, then a five-layer account of market infrastructure is not a four-layer account plus context. It is an account of five infrastructures, one of which happens to be made of relationships.Economic sociology supplies the mechanism. Granovetter (1985) established that economic action is embedded in concrete networks of relations. Portes and Sensenbrenner (1993) then did the analytical work that the embeddedness literature most often omits, distinguishing four mechanisms by which social structure shapes economic action and, crucially, identifying their positive and negative consequences together. Value introjection and bounded solidarity generate commitment and mutual support but also generate demands for conformity. Reciprocity exchanges and enforceable trust lower transaction costs but also impose obligations that can drain the successful and restrict the individual autonomy on which enterprise growth depends. Portes and Landolt (1996) and Portes (1998) developed the resulting downsides, namely exclusion of outsiders, excess claims on group members, restrictions on individual freedom and downward levelling norms. We adopt this four-mechanism decomposition as the analytical core of our framework, because it is what allows a symmetrical reading of communal institutions rather than a celebratory one.Two further strands complete the framing. The contextualisation programme in entrepreneurship research insists that where and when entrepreneurship happens is constitutive rather than incidental (Welter, 2011;Welter et al., 2019), and Kloosterman's (2010) mixed embeddedness perspective shows how the resources an entrepreneur can mobilise from social networks interact with the opportunity structure that markets and regulation supply. Meanwhile, the entrepreneurial ecosystem literature has become the dominant policy vocabulary for the phenomena we describe, and its own systematic reviews concede that it remains largely atheoretical and built on advanced-economy assumptions, with resource scarcity, structural gaps and institutional voids distinguishing emergingeconomy ecosystems (Cao and Shi, 2021;Wurth et al., 2022). Our framework is intended in part as a sociological supplement to that literature, replacing its metaphor of an ecosystem of actors with an account of layered infrastructures and the filters that regulate access to them.By market infrastructure we mean the bundle of arrangements that allow a small firm to find customers, set prices, secure finance, manage logistics and enforce rights. We distinguish five layers. The physical layer covers roads, warehouses, bazaars and border posts. The financial layer covers banks, microfinance, payment instruments and credit lines. The digital layer covers e-commerce, platform identifiers, e-government and data systems (Nambisan, 2017;Bonina et al., 2021). The institutional layer covers registration, taxation, standards and dispute resolution. The social layer covers trust networks, reputational systems, professional associations, rotating savings groups and the mahalla.The analytically important claim is not the existence of five layers but the relation between them. Access to any of the first four layers is mediated through the fifth, and the fifth distributes that access unequally. A credit assessment reads a reputation that is produced in a network. A customs procedure is navigated with the help of brokers and peers who have navigated it before. A digital marketplace is adopted first by entrepreneurs whose existing ties already include early users, which is why platform adoption tends to follow pre-existing network structure rather than to disrupt it (Bonina et al., 2021).Where public investment addresses the first four layers without engaging the fifth, returns are eroded by filtering rather than by underprovision. The new road serves the bazaar of the better connected. The new credit line reaches firms with formal collateral. The new platform recruits younger urban men with smartphones and foreign-language skills. This is the splintering dynamic that Graham and Marvin (2001) described, produced here by social rather than commercial sorting.Urban evidence from Uzbekistan supports this reading at the level of the layers themselves. Farmanov et al. (2025), examining smart-city implementation in Bukhara, find that deployment of sensors, platforms and digital governance tools has run ahead of the inclusivity and citizen-engagement components, so that a technically advancing infrastructure is not correspondingly more usable. Dushanova et al. (2025) document the same asymmetry in the city's tourism infrastructure, where heritage sites, transport and wayfinding remain inaccessible to people with mobility impairments despite a national policy commitment to barrier-free provision. Both cases show a filter that is not social in the network sense but produces the same result, namely infrastructure that is formally universal and practically selective. They also support treating market infrastructure as a sociotechnical assembly rather than a technical one, which is the premise of Section 2.In the Uzbek case we identify five social mediators through which the filtering runs, namely mahalla networks, gender norms and the unpaid care burden, the urban-rural divide, the informal economy, and labour migration. These are not causes in a statistical sense and we do not claim to have estimated their effects. They are the channels through which formally universal infrastructure becomes differentially accessible, and Section 6 states precisely how much evidence stands behind each.Figure 1. Five-layer framework of market infrastructure for small entrepreneurship in Uzbekistan. Infrastructure layers reach policy outcomes only through social mediators. Each mediator has an enabling and a restricting side, corresponding to the four mechanisms of social capital in Portes and Sensenbrenner (1993). Which side dominates depends on the mechanism a given reform activates.mahalla solidarity has historically rested on residence rather than kinship or ethnicity, which gave it an unusually broad reach across social groups. Urinboyev and Eraliev (2022) describe the mahalla as a legally plural arena in which competing orders coexist and produce new organisational forms, some of them generative.On the restricting side, the record is at least as substantial and considerably older than our earlier draft acknowledged. Three findings matter for market infrastructure specifically.First, the mahalla's incorporation into public administration has converted an association of residents into an instrument of state administration and, in the assessment of a large body of work, of social control (Urinboyev, 2011;Noori, 2006;Human Rights Watch, 2003). Urinboyev and Eraliev (2022) situate this within broader debates on how non-democratic states neutralise civil-society institutions through administrative and legal incorporation. An entrepreneur's relationship with the mahalla is therefore not a purely horizontal relationship among peers. It carries a vertical dimension, and any policy that routes market infrastructure through the mahalla routes it through that vertical dimension too.Second, mahalla-based discretionary allocation has documented exclusionary effects along gender lines. Kamp (2004) shows that the delegation of welfare targeting to mahalla committees, staffed by untrained neighbours exercising discretion, placed divorced and abandoned women at particular risk of exclusion, and that solidarity among women in a mahalla cannot be assumed. This is bounded solidarity and enforceable trust operating exactly as Portes and Sensenbrenner predicted, producing support for insiders and exclusion at the boundary. If discretionary neighbourhood assessment produces this pattern in welfare, there is no principled reason to expect a different pattern when the same bodies certify cooperatives, endorse borrowers or vouch for exporters.Third, the conformity costs fall unevenly. Restrictions on individual autonomy and downward levelling norms are the two downsides of social capital most directly relevant to enterprise growth (Portes, 1998;Portes and Landolt, 1996). Ethnographic work on women traders in Uzbek bazaars describes exactly this tension, with women negotiating and renegotiating patriarchal norms rather than simply being enabled or simply being blocked by them (Kandiyoti, 2007).The implication for policy is that "recognise the mahalla" is an underspecified instruction. What matters is which mechanism a given reform activates. Instruments that work through reciprocity exchange, such as linking gap groups to formal microfinance, plausibly extend access. Instruments that work through discretionary gatekeeping, such as making mahalla endorsement a condition of registration, credit or certification, plausibly reproduce existing exclusions and add a vertical dependency. We return to this distinction in Section 7.A framework that applies identically to everyone explains nothing about distribution. Three points follow from the table. The binding constraint differs by position, so a single infrastructure package cannot be expected to have uniform effects. The same mechanism that helps one position hinders another, which is why a framework built on Portes and Sensenbrenner's symmetric account is more useful here than one built on social capital as an unambiguous good. And the reforms most likely to backfire are, in several rows, the reforms currently most favoured, namely discretionary community endorsement and platform-first digitalisation.Two of the three policy outcomes named in the title deserve explicit grounding, since the framework is meant to bear on them.Export concentration is documented. In 2024 gold, services and industrial goods together accounted for roughly 70 percent of total exports (Observatory of Economic Complexity, 2025; U.S. Department of Commerce, 2025), and the number of exporting enterprises stood at around 5,700 in mid-2024 against the 2030 target of 15,000 (Ministry of Investment and Foreign Trade, 2024). The shortfall is usually read as a logistics and certification problem. Our framework suggests it is also a trust problem, since enforceable trust built on personal relationship and cash does not travel across borders and infrastructure that supplies no substitute concentrates gains among firms already connected to international buyers. The concentration is a fact; its attribution to social filtering is our proposition.Employment is where the filters compound. items.title: In Pursuit of Ideal Data: Epistemic Enchantment and the Unintended Consequences of Datafying for Artificial Intelligence
items.abstract: The increasing datafication of work has become a pervasive theme within organizations, particularly with the rise of artificial intelligence (AI) technologies that rely on data and machine learning to generate insights and decisions. Prior research has shown that datafication practices aimed at administrative control and accountability can transform organizations in profound and often unintended ways. Our research moves beyond investigating datafication for administrative purposes to explore how it unfolds when actors intend to extract knowledge through AI predictive modeling. Drawing on a three-year ethnography of a human resources (HR) department introducing AI for candidate screening, we find that datafication expanded far beyond the technology’s initially envisioned scope. We explain this scope expansion by introducing the concept of epistemic enchantment : a collective process through which organizational members become captivated and mobilized by AI’s promise to generate predictive, objective, and continuously improving insights from data, while overlooking the costs and risks involved. Our study reveals how datafication practices can expand endlessly as organizational members, enchanted by AI’s epistemic promises, pursue the notion of ideal data as an ever-desired but never reachable goal.

items.title: Incremental Program Synthesis from Event Logs
items.abstract: The goal of program synthesis is to enable non-expert users to write programs by providing a specification instead of an implementation. To truly realize this goal, the specification must require no expertise and no effort to generate. We consider the problem of synthesizing automation scripts from only the logs that are automatically collected by many systems. Using our approach, users can automate tasks they usually perform manually, without having to know how to program them. Because logs are collected automatically, the synthesis approach needs to scale to large sets of logs. We present a new algorithm to solve this task by incrementally extending an API-calling script with behavior exemplified by a sequence of log events, adding one sequence at a time. By minimizing the program modifications at each step, we preserve user intent and synthesize a program as general as possible. We show that our approach, implemented in a tool LogLoom, scales to synthesis tasks with more traces and more complex programs than existing techniques. LogLoom synthesizes scripts that are identical to reference solutions for 60 out of 72 benchmarks, compared to 14 for an existing symbolic approach and 39 for an LLM.

items.title: Innovations in Teaching; the Implementation of ICT in the Teaching of Scientific and Artistic Subjects and their Impact on the Personalization of Learning
items.abstract: In modern education, the information and communication technologies are having an increasing impact on personalized learning. Their implementation responds to the digital transformation in our society and requires the development of digital literacy as a key competence of both teachers and students. In Mathematics, Physics, Music and Art education, individualizing learning is supported by selected tools such as GeoGebra, Corinth 3D, Musescore, Solfy or graphic editors (GIMP, Procreate, Adobe Fresco). They enable adaptive and personalized forms of learning, support visualization, creativity, and self-directed learning. Although artificial intelligence presents challenges related to overreliance, academic integrity, and the development of critical and creative thinking, Information and communication technologies (ICT) and Artificial Intelligencie (AI) technologies can enhance education by supporting visualization, collaboration, creativity, differentiated instruction, and personalized learning.

items.title: Innovative Process Reengineering Techniques for Maximizing Efficiency in Financial Institutions
items.abstract: Innovative process reengineering techniques are essential for financial institutions seeking to maximize efficiency and adapt to rapidly evolving market dynamics. This Review explores the key concepts and strategies involved in implementing such techniques. Financial institutions are constantly under pressure to enhance efficiency, reduce costs, and improve customer satisfaction. To achieve these goals, many institutions are turning to innovative process reengineering techniques. These techniques involve rethinking and redesigning existing processes to streamline operations, eliminate redundancies, and improve overall efficiency. One of the key concepts in innovative process reengineering is the use of technology to automate manual tasks and improve workflow efficiency. For example, robotic process automation (RPA) can be used to automate repetitive tasks, such as data entry and reconciliation, freeing up employees to focus on more value-added activities. Similarly, artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) can be used to analyze large volumes of data and generate insights that can inform decision-making and improve operational efficiency. Another important aspect of innovative process reengineering is the use of data analytics to identify inefficiencies and opportunities for improvement. By analyzing data from various sources, financial institutions can gain valuable insights into their operations and identify areas where processes can be streamlined or optimized. For example, data analytics can be used to identify bottlenecks in the loan approval process or inefficiencies in the customer onboarding process, allowing institutions to make targeted improvements. In addition to technology and data analytics, innovative process reengineering techniques also involve rethinking organizational structures and culture. Financial institutions need to foster a culture of continuous improvement and innovation, where employees are encouraged to identify and implement process improvements. This may involve changing the way teams are organized, promoting collaboration across departments, and empowering employees to take ownership of process improvement initiatives. Overall, innovative process reengineering techniques are essential for financial institutions looking to maximize efficiency and stay competitive in today's rapidly changing business environment. By embracing technology, data analytics, and a culture of innovation, financial institutions can streamline their operations, reduce costs, and improve customer satisfaction.

items.title: Insecure Coding Preferences in Long-Term Memory: Security Risks for LLM-Based Code Generation
items.abstract: LLM-based systems increasingly incorporate long-term memory to improve cross-session continuity. However, once insecure coding preferences are stored, they may silently influence security-critical decisions in subsequent generations. In this study, we conduct the first systematic empirical study on the impact of insecure coding preferences stored in long-term memory on the security of LLM-based code generation. We evaluate four LLMs (ChatGPT, Gemini, Qwen, and Grok) across five programming languages (Python, C, C++, Go, and JavaScript). Our results show that insecure memories significantly increase the risk of generating vulnerable code by 2.7-50.3 percentage points (pp). Moreover, they create a 5.4-14.0 percentage-point risk-warning gap, where warning-rate increases lag behind vulnerability-rate increases. Further analysis reveals that insecure memories are difficult to overwrite through normal interactions and can broadly influence model outputs even when prompts are phrased differently. Finally, we evaluate three mitigation strategies: security-requirement appending and memory storage reduce vulnerability rates by 19.7-33.6 pp but may degrade functional correctness by up to 15.9 pp; memory-level safety filtering achieves a 100% detection rate on our evaluated risky memory entries and restores generation behavior to the without-memory baseline. Based on these findings, we provide actionable suggestions to improve the security of long-term memory in LLM-based code generation.

items.title: Integrating AI-assisted design thinking in citizenship education: Enhancing university students’ problem analysis and critical thinking skills
items.abstract: This study aims to analyse the implementation of an AI-assisted design thinking learning model in enhancing university students’ problem analysis and critical thinking skills in Citizenship Education programmes. The study employed a qualitative approach involving undergraduate students from several Citizenship Education programmes at universities on Java Island, Indonesia. The learning implementation integrated artificial intelligence (AI) to assist students in exploring information, generating ideas and reflecting on solutions to civic and social issues. Research data were collected through observations of the learning process, analysis of students’ assignment documents, AI-assisted interaction records and group discussions conducted during the implementation of the model. Data were analysed descriptively to identify the dynamics of the learning process at each stage of design thinking. The findings indicate that AI-assisted design thinking encouraged students to engage actively in social problem analysis and problem-solving. During the empathise stage, students identified social issues through digital information exploration, AI use and group discussions, enabling them to understand problems from multiple perspectives. In the define stage, students formulated problems more systematically by identifying causal relationships and the underlying social contexts. The ideate stage encouraged students to generate alternative solutions creatively and collaboratively through group discussions and AI-supported idea development. In the prototype and test stages, students developed solution designs in the form of programmes or simple policy models and evaluated their effectiveness through reflection, feedback and AI-assisted analysis. The study concludes that AI supports, but does not replace, students’ critical reasoning, the quality of which depends on reflective pedagogical design.

items.title: Integrating Blockchain with AI: A Data-Driven Model for Secure, Scalable Decentralized Finance (DeFi) Systems
items.abstract: The rapid evolution of decentralized finance (DeFi) has ushered in transformative opportunities for global financial inclusion, digital asset management, and permissionless transactions. However, the growth of DeFi also presents significant challenges related to data integrity, security, scalability, and regulatory compliance. This paper proposes a novel datadriven model that integrates blockchain technology with artificial intelligence (AI) to address these challenges and optimize DeFi operations. By leveraging the transparency, immutability, and decentralization of blockchain in conjunction with AI's predictive analytics, automation, and pattern recognition capabilities, this integrated framework enhances the resilience, efficiency, and scalability of DeFi systems. The model introduces an intelligent smart contract ecosystem powered by AI algorithms for fraud detection, anomaly monitoring, and automated compliance auditing. Machine learning techniques are applied to real-time transactional data across decentralized exchanges (DEXs), liquidity pools, and lending platforms to identify suspicious behaviors and mitigate risks proactively. Furthermore, the use of blockchain ensures tamper-proof audit trails, consensus-driven trust, and transparent governance, thus increasing user confidence and institutional adoption. Scalability is addressed through the application of layer-2 blockchain solutions and AI-based resource optimization strategies, enabling faster transaction throughput and reduced latency. Privacy-preserving AI models such as federated learning and homomorphic encryption are integrated to maintain user confidentiality while allowing intelligent data analysis. The paper also highlights potential use cases in automated asset management, decentralized credit scoring, and cross-chain interoperability. This interdisciplinary approach presents a secure, adaptive, and scalable paradigm for the next generation of DeFi systems. It aligns with global trends toward decentralized digital economies and offers a robust foundation for financial innovation, especially in regions with limited access to traditional banking infrastructure. The paper concludes with a discussion of the model's implementation roadmap, potential limitations, and regulatory implications. The integration of blockchain with AI in DeFi offers not only technical advantages but also the potential to redefine trust, security, and efficiency in the global financial ecosystem.

items.title: Integration of Artificial Intelligence into Architectural Education: An Online Model Proposal for Instructor Training for Studio Courses
items.abstract: Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) is driving a fundamental paradigm shift in architectural design, transitioning from deterministic drafting to algorithmic curation. While the Architecture, Engineering, and Construction (AEC) sector rapidly adopts these tools, academic curricula face a “Techno-Instructional Void.” This gap risks inducing a “Zero Order Thinking State” (ZOTS)—a cognitive passivity rooted in Cognitive Load Theory, where students uncritically accept unbuildable machine hallucinations. To address this, we applied a Design and Development Research (DDR Type 2) methodology to build a conceptual framework. It revolves around the “Twin Houses” andragogy and the “Technical Sealing” protocol. By enforcing “Cognitive Friction,” the framework compels students to validate probabilistic GenAI outputs against ergonomic constants (such as Blondel’s Formula) and safety norms. We intentionally reject automated AI-to-BIM pipelines. Instead, the model turns Building Information Modeling (BIM) into an active Proof-Assistant. Learners have to manually and parametrically rationalize their AI-generated ideas utilizing visual programming APIs (Revit Dynamo, Allplan PythonParts) and IFC 4.3 data schemas for rigorous Rule-Based Checking (RBC). Formal expert validation interviews (n = 5) and empirical observations of Turkish student design cases support this theoretical model. While we initially noted autoethnographic evidence of institutional resistance across certain European academic ecosystems, the model subsequently secured preliminary external support from a leading institution in Germany. Ultimately, this framework provides a structured andragogical approach, equipping instructors to guide students in understanding how probabilistic algorithmic outputs can be systematically translated into buildable tectonic realities when subjected to rigorous deterministic technical validation.

items.title: Inteligencia sin comprensión. Magnifica Humanitas: de las dos ausencias de la máquina y la custodia de la persona
items.abstract: This article examines the central claim of the encyclical Magnifica Humanitas (2026), namely that artificial intelligence is fundamentally different from human intelligence and that, therefore, the human person requires special protection. Drawing on epistemology, philosophy of mind, and Kantian thought, the author argues that contemporary AI systems are marked by two fundamental limitations: they lack understanding and experience. Although they can generate convincing and useful responses, they do not grasp the conceptual relations that structure human knowledge, nor do they possess the lived experience through which the world acquires meaning. Based on these absences, the article introduces the concept of conversational heteronomy, understood as the gradual replacement of personal judgment by conclusions generated by systems that neither reason nor experience as subjects. The study concludes that the ethical challenge is not to reject artificial intelligence, but to employ it without surrendering the distinctly human capacities to understand, experience, and judge, thereby preserving moral autonomy and human dignity.

items.title: Intelligent Knowledge Management in Water Treatment: A Scientometric Analysis of Thematic Trends, Collaboration Networks, Research Gaps, and Future Research Priorities
items.abstract: Purpose: Knowledge management (KM) is recognized as a critical strategic framework that enables organizations to effectively leverage intellectual assets and enhance operational efficiency. In the water treatment industry, KM involves the collection, organization, sharing, and utilization of employees’ technical knowledge and specialized expertise. This process promotes technological innovation, increases system productivity, and improves service quality. Recently, the role of KM in organizations, including the water sector, has evolved to become closely integrated with artificial intelligence (AI). This development has garnered significant scholarly attention, leading to a growing body of research. One of the most effective methods to evaluate these research outputs is scientometric analysis. Therefore, this study examines scientific production in the field of intelligent KM in water treatment, aiming to identify thematic trends, collaboration networks, research gaps, and future research priorities.Methodology: This applied research utilizes scientometric techniques to analyze scientific publications related to intelligent knowledge management (KM) in water purification. Relevant articles were retrieved from the Scopus and Web of Science databases. From an initial pool of 172 documents, 49 were selected after screening titles, abstracts, and keywords. Scientometric analyses were performed using the bibliometrix package in R. To address the research questions, bibliometric methods and word co-occurrence networks were employed. Frequent keywords were identified, dominant conceptual clusters were mapped, and influential thematic trends were examined. Additionally, strategic diagrams, thematic mapping, and hierarchical clustering were used to construct a comprehensive science map of the field.Findings: Since 2015, there has been an increasing focus on knowledge management in this field. In 2024, the highest number of documents was published, totaling eight scientific productions. Other notable years include 2022 and 2018, with seven and five articles published, respectively, demonstrating a growing trend. China, the United States, and the United Kingdom were the most active countries, contributing 11, 10, and 6 scientific documents, respectively. Beijing University of Technology and Tianjin University have played crucial roles in generating knowledge and advancing new technologies in this area. The journal IEEE Transactions on Industrial Informatics, with three articles, ranks first among sources publishing documents, with most sources classified as Q1. The top researchers, Han Honggui and Qiao Junfei, each have four articles, while Wu Xiaolong has three, highlighting their significant contributions to research knowledge production. Vocabulary analysis and topic trends indicate that artificial intelligence, machine learning, environmental monitoring, and intelligent systems are the most frequently discussed subjects. The trend chart reveals a progression in topics within this field, beginning with decision support systems and water purification, transitioning to water management and decision-making supported by knowledge management systems, and ultimately focusing on artificial intelligence and system training through machine learning. Hierarchical clustering has identified three thematic axes: water resources management and safe water supply through new technologies; the emergence of new technologies and support systems; and water quality monitoring through system training. Strategic topics such as wastewater treatment, data mining, decision support systems, and knowledge management are considered mature areas that will shape future research directions. Additionally, topics like denitrification, nitrogen removal, and freshwater resource management are fundamental to supporting the main research axes. Climate change, cost-effectiveness, ecosystems, and water pollution are highlighted as emerging or declining topics. Quality control, environmental monitoring, and the aquatic environment occupy central positions in the diagram, acting as bridges between core topics and driving forces in the field.Conclusion: The findings indicate that the field of intelligent KM in water treatment has achieved relative stability in recent years and continues to maintain a strong position within interdisciplinary research. Analysis shows that core topics—including KM, data mining, intelligent organizations, and advanced water treatment technologies—remain central to scholarly attention and play a crucial role in optimizing treatment processes. Emerging trends suggest a multidimensional evolution, with the convergence of KM and advanced technologies offering pathways to enhance water quality, promote environmental sustainability, and reduce costs, time, and energy consumption. Strengthening international collaboration, expanding scientific networks, and adopting AI-, machine learning–, and data mining–based approaches can further consolidate and advance the field. In summary, the future of research related to knowledge management in water purification will depend on the use of smart technologies, extensive global interactions, holding global conferences in this field, and effective participation in international scientific cooperation.

items.title: Intelligent Rock Tunnel Engineering: Reframing the Industry With Signal Processing and Artificial Intelligence
items.abstract: ABSTRACT The transformation of rock tunnel engineering (RTE), a pivotal component of modern infrastructure, is driven by advances in signal processing and artificial intelligence (AI). This review synthesizes the existing literature to examine how time‐series, image, and manually collected data are acquired, preprocessed, and utilized in RTE. These data are applied to various aspects, including geotechnical property analysis, construction optimization, safety assurance, and operational maintenance optimization. We summarize the core algorithms and identify prevailing challenges such as data heterogeneity and data silos. Future research should focus on multi‐source data fusion and large models, while microseismic‐based rock‐burst prediction also warrants further exploration. Overall, the fusion of signal processing and AI significantly enhances the efficiency, accuracy, and safety of tunnel projects, offering a robust pathway towards sustainable next‐generation underground infrastructure.

items.title: Interdisciplinary Colloquium on Digitalisation of Research: "Why so serious? Generative AI (genAI) in Knowledge-Work from a Text-Workers' Perspective" 2026.10.01 with Janine Gondolf and Clemens Ackerl
items.abstract: Generative AI (genAI) systems have become an integral part of scientific text-producing practice. They can conduct literature-related research, organize content and information, proofread text, and assist with writing itself. Above all, they are credited with reducing workload by taking on or taking over these routine tasks. Drawing on an internal, interdisciplinary KIT-ITAS project that deployed the genAI-supported research assistance system 'Undermind.ai', we demonstrate that the potential to reduce workload is offset by the need to reorganize basic scientific competencies in response to the changing workflow requirements of genAI-assisted knowledge work. GenAI systems produce texts that closely resemble stylistic conventions and appear both well-formed and plausible. However, the closer these texts adhere to researchers’ expectations, the more challenging it becomes to verify their content using established academic methods. This generates higher-order efforts that must be weighed against existing working standards for assessing text-based results. The constant validation and ongoing negotiation of plausibility with the system’s output, both during and beyond the writing process, places additional demands on researchers’ critical competence and judgement. Using genAI in knowledge work thus shifts the focus of familiar textual and intellectual labour practices and procedures away from independent creation and toward the verification of textual output, along with the corresponding demands on epistemic attention, responsibility, authorization, and authority.

items.title: Interdisciplinary Colloquium on Digitalisation of Research: "Why so serious? Generative AI (genAI) in Knowledge-Work from a Text-Workers' Perspective" 2026.10.01 with Janine Gondolf and Clemens Ackerl
items.abstract: Generative AI (genAI) systems have become an integral part of scientific text-producing practice. They can conduct literature-related research, organize content and information, proofread text, and assist with writing itself. Above all, they are credited with reducing workload by taking on or taking over these routine tasks. Drawing on an internal, interdisciplinary KIT-ITAS project that deployed the genAI-supported research assistance system 'Undermind.ai', we demonstrate that the potential to reduce workload is offset by the need to reorganize basic scientific competencies in response to the changing workflow requirements of genAI-assisted knowledge work. GenAI systems produce texts that closely resemble stylistic conventions and appear both well-formed and plausible. However, the closer these texts adhere to researchers’ expectations, the more challenging it becomes to verify their content using established academic methods. This generates higher-order efforts that must be weighed against existing working standards for assessing text-based results. The constant validation and ongoing negotiation of plausibility with the system’s output, both during and beyond the writing process, places additional demands on researchers’ critical competence and judgement. Using genAI in knowledge work thus shifts the focus of familiar textual and intellectual labour practices and procedures away from independent creation and toward the verification of textual output, along with the corresponding demands on epistemic attention, responsibility, authorization, and authority.

items.title: Internet of things-enabled biomedical engineering: current applications, challenges, and emerging directions
items.abstract: The internet of medical things (IoMT) is a structured integrative review of the internet of things (IoT) that focuses on the medical field, specifically on the integration of physiological sensors, medical devices, communication networks, and the clinical information systems to monitor and track patients' health and conditions continuously, and use data to support medical treatment. Through July 2026, a reproducible search and evidence audit of PubMed/MEDLINE, IEEE Xplore, Google Scholar, publisher/digital object identifier (DOI) records, and authoritative regulatory and standards repositories was conducted. The final evidence base consisted of 65 distinct sources that were assessed using a set of explicit eligibility criteria and evidence weighting. Wearable atrial-fibrillation screening, remote monitoring, digital inhalers and continuous glucose monitoring (CGM), and connected hospital infrastructure were shown to be clinically significant in large-scale studies, but such benefits were only seen if there was confirmatory pathway, workflow integration, data quality and persistent engagement. Cybersecurity, privacy, interoperability, validation, workforce capacity, equity, and lifecycle sustainability were all key challenges. The review also brought a synthesis and readiness framework that connects edge artificial intelligence (AI), federated learning, digital twins, advanced connectivity, and circular lifecycle management with measurable validation and governance requirements across the domains.

items.title: Investigating the Effect of Spatial AR Linear Visual Cues on Positioning and Alignment in Teleoperated Robotic Manipulation
items.abstract: Teleoperation is critical for lunar maintenance, yet limited visual feedback often impairs depth perception and precise robotic control. This study quantitatively evaluates three Augmented Reality (AR) guidance schemes (fundamental Vertical-Extension and Connection primitives, alongside our newly proposed Combined Lines) against a control baseline during 6-DOF robotic arm insertion tasks within a high-fidelity VR simulation. Both objective performance metrics and subjective workload were analyzed. Results demonstrate that AR conditions generally outperformed the baseline, drastically reducing spatial errors and failure rates. Among successfully completed trials, the proposed Combined Lines condition showed advantages in alignment accuracy while yielding the lowest cognitive load. Notably, these advantages varied with the maintenance-panel angle, with clearer alignment advantages for Combined Lines at 45° and 135°. These findings offer empirical guidelines for designing user-centered AR interfaces to enhance spatial awareness and operational safety in constrained remote environments.

items.title: IoT-Based Water Quality Monitoring and Demand Prediction for Sustainable Management
items.abstract: Water resource management has become an increasingly critical issue due to rapid urbanization, population growth, climate variability, and industrial expansion. Ensuring a sustainable water supply requires not only effective distribution but also accurate prediction of future water demand and continuous monitoring of water quality. In this study, we explore the application of Artificial Intelligence (AI) and Machine Learning (ML) models to predict water consumption patterns based on historical data and influential factors such as population dynamics, temperature fluctuations, and rainfall variability. We implemented and evaluated three predictive models—Linear Regression, Random Forest, and Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) Neural Networks—by comparing their prediction accuracy, computational efficiency, and error metrics including Mean Absolute Error (MAE) and Root Mean Square Error (RMSE). Among these, the LSTM model outperformed the others, achieving high predictive accuracies of 0.88 for daily, 0.87 for monthly, and 0.86 for yearly forecasts, alongside a significantly low MAE of 1.5 and RMSE of 1.90. The LSTM model’s ability to capture complex temporal dependencies in water usage data demonstrates its suitability for real-world forecasting applications. Furthermore, we propose that the integration of Internet of Things (IoT) technologies—such as sensor networks for real-time monitoring of pH levels, turbidity, flow rates, and pressure—can further enhance the model's responsiveness and predictive capabilities. AI-driven water management frameworks can optimize distribution schedules, detect leaks early, monitor pollution events, and support proactive decision-making, ultimately promoting sustainable urban and rural water systems. Future work will explore hybrid deep learning approaches, cloud-based data analytics, and real-time adaptive control systems to create more intelligent and resilient water management infrastructures. The outcomes of this research offer significant potential for government agencies, water utility companies, and smart city initiatives aiming to achieve sustainable and efficient water resource management in the face of growing environmental and socioeconomic pressures.
